What Is Space Radiation?
Outside Earth’s protective magnetic field and atmosphere, the ionizing radiation in space will pose a serious risk to astronauts as they travel to Mars. High-energy galactic cosmic rays, which are remnants from supernovas, and solar storms like solar particle events and coronal mass ejections can harm the body and spacecraft. When astronauts travel in space, they can’t see or even feel radiation. However, NASA scientists are studying the effects radiation plays on the human body and developing ways to monitor and protect against this silent hazard.
Radiation is energy emitted in the form of rays, electromagnetic waves, and particles. In some cases, radiation can be seen (visible light) or felt (infrared radiation), while other forms—like x-rays and gamma rays—are not visible and can only be observed with special equipment. Although radiation can have negative effects both on biological and mechanical systems, it can also be carefully used to learn more about each of those systems.
Radiation exposure increases cancer risk, damages the central nervous system, can alter cognitive function, reduce motor function, and prompt behavioral changes. To learn what can happen above low-Earth orbit, NASA studies how radiation affects biological samples using a ground-based research laboratory.

title: Hazard: Gravity Fields
prompt: What are the physiological and mission impacts of the NASA spaceflight hazard: Hazard: Gravity Fields?
response:
Floating weightlessly within a spacecraft can lead to dizziness, bone and muscle loss, vision issues, and more. Astronauts may also need time to adjust to new gravity fields after landing on the Moon or Mars before they conduct mission-critical tasks. Developing strategies that enable crew members to adapt quickly to different gravitational fields will be key to mission success.
Astronauts will encounter three different gravity fields on a Mars mission. On the six-month trek between the planets, crews will be weightless. While living and working on Mars, crews will be in approximately one-third of Earth’s gravity. Finally, upon returning home, crews will have to readapt to Earth’s gravity.
Switching from one gravity field to another is trickier than it sounds. The transition affects spatial orientation, head-eye and hand-eye coordination, balance, and locomotion, with some crew members experiencing space motion sickness.
Landing a spacecraft on Mars could be challenging as astronauts adjust to the gravity field of another celestial body. When shifting from weightlessness to gravity, astronauts may even experience lightheadedness and fainting.
Without the continuous load of Earth’s gravity, weight-bearing bones lose on average 1% to 1.5% of mineral density per month during spaceflight. Water and other fluids in the body shift upward to the head, which may put pressure on the eyes and cause vision problems. If preventive measures are not implemented, crews may experience an increased risk of developing kidney stones due to dehydration and increased excretion of calcium from their bones.

title: Hazard: Hostile/Closed Environments
prompt: What are the physiological and mission impacts of the NASA spaceflight hazard: Hazard: Hostile/Closed Environments?
response:
Maintaining a safe ecosystem inside a vehicle presents unique challenges, from ensuring optimal temperatures, pressures, and lighting, to reducing noise, monitoring microbial communities, and tracking immune responses.
The ecosystem inside a spacecraft plays a big role in the daily life of an astronaut in space.
Microbes can change characteristics in space, and micro-organisms that naturally live on the human body are transferred more easily from person to person in closed habitats, such as the space station. Stress hormone levels can elevate and the immune system can alter, which could lead to increased susceptibility to allergies or other illnesses. More research is needed into whether these changes pose serious risks to astronauts.
Beyond the effects of the environment on the immune system, every inch and detail of living and working quarters must be carefully considered and designed. No one wants their house to be too hot, too cold, cramped, crowded, loud, or poorly lit, and no one would enjoy working and living in such a habitat in space either.

title: Risk of Bone Fracture due to Spaceflight-induced Changes to Bone
prompt: Explain NASA HRP Risk #77 (Bone Fracture): Risk of Bone Fracture due to Spaceflight-induced Changes to Bone, its mission ratings, and clinical context.
response:
HRP Element: Human Health Countermeasures (HHC). Risk Statement: Given the skeletal changes that occur during spaceflight, there is a possibility that the bones of crewmembers during and after spaceflight are not as strong as they were before spaceflight and a fracture may occur postflight for activities otherwise unlikely to induce fracture prior to space flight. HSRB State of Knowledge Fracture risk (Ops) increases with likelihood of applied loads to bone > bone strength. Fracture risk (Long-Term Health (LTH)) is focused on detection of skeletal fragility. Low areal Bone Mineral Density (aBMD) has been widely used to assess skeletal fragility due to age-related bone loss. Diagnosis by aBMD is recognized by terrestrial medicine to be insufficient (requires monitoring index of Bone Quality), especially for males <50 years and pre-menopausal females. Extensive pre/post flight aBMD measurements exist for International Space Station (ISS) astronauts; exercise regimens using ARED/T2 (Advanced Resistive Exercise Device/Treadmill 2) six days/week have minimized deficits in postflight aBMDs. Notably, the minimum aBMD Permissible Outcome Limit (POL) for bone health was met before ARED/T2 were implemented on the ISS suggesting that postflight aBMD alone is not useful as a POL. Measured changes in putative biomarkers of Bone Quality, e.g., trabecular bone, whole bone structure, and estimates of bone strength, with and without pharmaceuticals, are limited to research studies. Mitigation Strategy While there are ongoing research activities on this risk, the Human Research Program currently has no plans to solicit for or pursue any new research projects in this area. The definition of fracture risk in astronauts is grounded in the ability to estimate the probability of fractures. In particular, there are two broad categories of fractures in astronauts that can be identified: 1)“atraumatic” fractures – which are due to a severely depressed level of bone strength that results in fractures with minimal to no loading to bone and 2) “traumatic” fractures – which are due to mechanical loads applied to bone that exceed the strength of bones (i.e., biomechanical capacity or competence). Atraumatic fractures are more likely to occur during long-term health (LTH ) while traumatic fractures would more likely occur during physical activities under the hazardous or mechanically-loaded conditions of planetary surfaces (OPS and after return to Earth). The inability to monitor when skeletal bones have reached a level of deconditioning that compromises the strength of bones also contributes to increased fracture risk during OPS. Because the probability of fracture influences the type and timing of mitigating countermeasure, it becomes critical to 1) fully characterize the effects of spaceflight on skeletal tissue to assess the overall condition of bones (informing estimates of bone strength) and 2) develop tools and tests to inform the Factor of Fracture Risk (where FOR=Applied Loads/Bone Strength) focusing on physical activities and/or hazards during and after spaceflight. Hence, irrespective of type or timing of fractures (OPS or LTH), a key to a Mitigation Strategy is to pursue fuller characterization of spaceflight-induced skeletal changes . It is more likely that a long-duration spaceflight of at least 100 days would induce detectable changes in bone densitometry in astronauts because it approximates the duration of one bone remodeling cycle. The measurement of areal bone mineral density (aBMD) by Dual–energy X-ray Absorptiometry (DXA) is the terrestrial clinical test for diagnosing primary osteoporosis (skeletal fragility due to age-related bone loss); this test is performed triennially in active and retired astronauts to surveil for premature fragility (relative to fragility resulting from age-related bone loss) as a risk factor for LTH fractures in astronauts. Additionally, serial DXA measurements at NASA, performed before and after long-duration spaceflights, have also been expressed as a % change from preflight aBMD. This metric is used consequently by NASA to describe the skeletal effects of spaceflight on bones, to evaluate the efficacy of in-flight countermeasures and to monitor restoration to baseline (preflight) status. Mitigation strategies have been typically evaluated by their ability to mitigate negative % changes or, alternatively stated, an ability to preserve astronauts’ bones at their preflight status. As previously mentioned, NASA could assess the risk for traumatic OPS fractures, i.e., associated with physical activities during a mission, by estimating a Factor of Risk (FOR). A FOR quantifies the ratio of applied loads to bone strength (FOR=Applied Loads/Bone Strength) where a FOR > 1 indicates fracture occurrence. Calculating a FOR involves estimating when applied loads to bones (during the performance of mission activities or with physical activities after return to Earth) might exceed the ability of bones to resist failure (i.e., fracture). A Probabilistic Risk Assessment for fractures during NASA design reference missions –which uses DXA measured-BMD as the index for bone strength, -- has been completed in support of the Integrated Medical Model. Based upon this analysis (which integrates the uncertainty and limitations of modeling tools), the probability of fracture is considered low for all Design Reference Missions and the NASA Human System Risk Board has deemed the Fracture risk for OPS to be “accepted.” Characterization of spaceflight-induced changes to bone are being expanded with new research approaches (i.e., supplementing measurement of DXA aBMD to enhance the FOR estimations of bone strength and fracture probability). Even though clinical guidelines for using novel skeletal measurements (i.e., of Bone Quality) to predict fractures are not as developed as with DXA aBMD, some skeletal changes in astronauts are notable, have been validated as predictors of fractures, and may warrant consideration for inclusion in countermeasure testing and in post-flight surveillance. In particular, there is some concern over the absence of full recovery to preflight skeletal measurements; astronauts may be predisposed to LTH fractures if deficits due to spaceflight were allowed to persist and combine with the deficits that develop due to aging. The gold standard metric for increased skeletal fragility (i.e., osteoporosis) is increased fracture incidence. However, due to limited subject numbers (<100 long-duration astronauts) and the younger-ages of astronauts (a prolonged time before fracture manifestation), the current number of LTH fractures is low. An in-depth epidemiological analysis of fracture incidence in astronauts is being updated. Recently, an analysis of fractures surveyed across all astronauts indicates that hip and lumbar spine fractures occur at higher count in the person-years following first exposure to a single long-duration mission (typically 180 days or greater) (Presented Am Soc Bone Mineral Research Sept. 2022, Austin, TX; manuscript submitted for publication Sept. 2024)). Six-month ISS missions in low Earth orbit have not resulted in a diagnosis of primary osteoporosis in returning astronauts, although the osteoporosis risk is very low in non-flying humans of similar age to astronauts. The loss of hip bone mass in ISS astronauts is not fully prevented by resistive exercise and may require additional countermeasures, verified for anti-resorptive effects, to protect the trabecular bone compartment. Lastly, it still remains to be determined if bone changes will stabilize or continue to diminish beyond 6 months.

title: Risk of Renal Stone Formation
prompt: Explain NASA HRP Risk #81 (Renal Stone): Risk of Renal Stone Formation, its mission ratings, and clinical context.
response:
HRP Element: Exploration Medical Capability (ExMC). Risk Statement: Given changes in urinary biochemistry during spaceflight, there is a possibility that symptomatic renal stones will occur, which could cause renal colic (pain), nausea, vomiting, hematuria, infection, and/or hydronephrosis. HSRB State of Knowledge Astronauts are at risk of developing symptomatic renal stones in- and post-flight. Risk mitigation strategies are well-defined although the ability to treat a renal stone during exploration missions is not yet available. Ground bedrest & immobilization studies indicate that exercise is a good countermeasure (CM) to lower urinary calcium cation (Ca2+) and that exercise also increases sweating providing an alternate route for Ca2+ release; therefore, exercise should be counted as a valid/current countermeasure. Randall’s plaques as a predictor for stone formation and in-flight ultrasound are areas for research and application. Mitigation Strategy Historical spaceflight data have revealed both in-flight and post-flight instances of renal stones. While none have led to loss of crew life, there have been in flight medical conditions leading to either evacuation or early termination of mission. Renal stone formation in microgravity has been well studied and modeled. Recent results from simulations starting with the chemistry of renal stone formation and ending with associated risk have provided validated models quantifying the risk of clinically significant renal stones during exploration as a function of hydration, nutritional countermeasures, and gravitational environment. Current research efforts are aimed at 1) integrating in-flight strategies to reduce stone formation into exploration medical system designs, 2) progressively autonomous ultrasound monitoring and biochemical diagnostics for early detection of stones, and 3) treatment interventions, such as moving renal stones through the application of ultrasound waves.

title: Risk of Adverse In-Mission Health and Performance Effects and Long-Term Health Effects Due to Celestial Dust Exposure
prompt: Explain NASA HRP Risk #82 (Dust): Risk of Adverse In-Mission Health and Performance Effects and Long-Term Health Effects Due to Celestial Dust Exposure, its mission ratings, and clinical context.
response:
HRP Element: Exploration Medical Capability (ExMC). Risk Statement: Given the unique properties of lunar and other celestial bodies' dust, there is a possibility that exposure could lead to serious health effects (e.g., respiratory, cardiopulmonary, ocular or dermal harm) or to crew performance impacts during celestial body missions. HSRB State of Knowledge NASA rodent-based research results coupled with expert review has determined that for six months of episodic exposure to lunar dust the exposure standard (NASA STD 3001, Volume 2) should be 0.3 mg/m3, which is tailorable based on mission exposure duration. This standard is based on inhalation toxicity studies of lunar dust (actual Apollo 14 samples with low crystalline silica content and characterized for heavy metals) and assumes that the exposure period is episodic and limited to the time before ECLSS can remove the particles from the internal atmosphere (assumed as 8 hours post-introduction). The recommended standard protects the respiratory system from injury caused by inhaled lunar dust and is set to also be adequately protective of other relevant health endpoints. This standard recognizes that lunar dust particles will likely deposit more in the peripheral areas of the lung compared to Earth gravity, but assumes this is offset by equivalent reductions in overall dust loading; an assumption that is subject to further scientific research. This standard may be refined, or new standards created for other celestial body dust exposure-based dust composition and mission profile. Lunar polar ice/subsurface regolith may contain volatiles of toxicological concern (e.g., mercury, ammonia, hydrogen sulfide) that are unlikely to be retained in dust on suits, etc., but will need to be assessed to ensure appropriate containment if samples are being stored in a habitable environment. Weight of evidence does not suggest a likely allergen challenge, although this potential is difficult to rule out entirely. Mitigation Strategy The impact of exposure to dust from extraterrestrial sources (celestial dusts) could lead to respiratory, cardiac, ocular, or dermal harm during exploration surface missions, resulting in immediate or long-term health effects. NASA needs to sufficiently characterize the consequences of exposure to these dusts so that vehicles and habitats are designed to maintain concentrations of airborne dust within safe limits while future operations planning minimizes the dust impacts on human health and performance. NASA rodent based research results coupled with expert review have established a permissible exposure limit (PEL) for lunar dust that has been converted into a NASA standard. This lunar dust NASA standard is being used to develop engineering controls for lunar surface missions that keep astronaut exposures below the PEL. Current research is focused on determining the allergenicity of lunar dust exposure and future work will be performed on Mars surface samples once acquired.

title: Risk of Mission Impacting Injury and Compromised Performance and Long-Term Health Effects due to EVA Operations
prompt: Explain NASA HRP Risk #84 (EVA): Risk of Mission Impacting Injury and Compromised Performance and Long-Term Health Effects due to EVA Operations, its mission ratings, and clinical context.
response:
HRP Element: Human Health Countermeasures (HHC). Risk Statement: Given the high-performance physiological and functional demands of operating in a self-contained EVA or training suit in various gravity fields and system environments, there is a possibility that crew injury and compromised physiological and functional performance may occur. HSRB State of Knowledge NASA-STD-3001: NASA Spaceflight Human-System Standard Vol 1: Crew Health and Vol 2: Human Factors, Habitability, and Environmental Health and NASA/SP-2010-3407, Human Integration Design Handbook (HIDH): suit life support and basic functionality; HIDH includes observed metabolic rates and human factors; no suit-induced operational injury prevention or operations guidance. Training injury data available, but injury mechanisms and associated individual risk factors (sex, anthropometry, fitness, etc.) are not yet understood. Microgravity EVA performance is characterized, but the physiological and functional demands of planetary EVAs are not understood, outside of a limited number of Lunar and Mars sites, where humans and robotic landers have been. Mitigation Strategy EVA preparedness and performance must be characterized as functions of gravitational field transitions and associated sensorimotor adaptations, as well as physical and cognitive fitness during operations requiring high operational tempos of surface EVAs. Adequate characterization will allow for development of countermeasures to combat sensorimotor deficits and physiologic decrements, initially by establishing techniques to monitor and promote general crew readiness. Additionally, the risks of DCS and hypoxia must be characterized to ensure that effects from living in a hypobaric, hypoxic environment (to enable rapid, frequent EVAs) do not exacerbate any negative health or performance-related effects. Characterization of human performance capabilities, as well as validation and operationalization of prebreathe protocols, in lower pressure habitats and elevated pressure spacesuits will serve to sufficiently mitigate risks to individual crewmembers and mission objectives. An overarching approach for mitigation of the EVA risk is outlined in the most recent version of the Integrated EVA Human Research Plan (currently here: https://www.nasa.gov/sites/default/files/atoms/files/tp-20205007604.pdf) .”

prompt: Explain NASA HRP Risk #85 (Immune): Risk of In Mission Impacts, Adverse Health Events or Long-Term Health Impacts due to Altered Immune Response, its mission ratings, and clinical context.
response:
HRP Element: Human Health Countermeasures (HHC). Risk Statement: Given that exposure to orbital spaceflight results in persistent dysregulation of the immune system, which leads to reactivation of latent herpesviruses and likely to an increased clinical incidence, including rashes and hypersensitivity reactions, there is a possibility that crewmembers will be susceptible to certain diseases during exploration class missions or long term health impacts. HSRB State of Knowledge Subclinical altered human immune function has been documented in crewmembers post-flight & in-flight (cytokine shifts, cell distribution shifts, specific changes in viral immunity or reactivation of latent viruses). These immune changes persist for the duration of a 6 month orbital flight. On-orbit clinical issues believed related to persistent immune dysregulation include increased incidence of skin rashes, various infectious processes and continued shedding of latent herpesviruses. Alterations to the immune function due to long duration missions is unknown. Future countermeasures may include: Operational procedures, functional foods, nutritional supplements, nutraceuticals, probiotics, pharmaceuticals, exercise, vaccination, behavioral countermeasures, bone countermeasures, personalized/precision medicine. Mitigation Strategy Prevent, monitor, and mitigate spaceflight-induced impaired immunity to protect in-mission health and performance (e.g., new infection, reactivation of dormant infection, autoimmune conditions, inflammation, hypersensitivity/rash) and long-term health (e.g., malignancies).

title: Risk of Altered Sensorimotor/Vestibular Function Impacting Critical Mission Tasks, Human Health, and Long-Term Health
prompt: Explain NASA HRP Risk #88 (Sensorimotor): Risk of Altered Sensorimotor/Vestibular Function Impacting Critical Mission Tasks, Human Health, and Long-Term Health, its mission ratings, and clinical context.
response:
HRP Element: Human Health Countermeasures (HHC). Risk Statement: Given that altered gravity leads to changes in sensorimotor/vestibular function that manifest in motion sickness, spatial disorientation, decrements in postural control and locomotion, and manual and fine motor control deficits, there is a possibility that crew will experience performance decrements in manual/vehicle control, extravehicular activities, and egress during and following these transitions and long-term health effects. HSRB State of Knowledge It has been shown that long duration spaceflight alters sensorimotor function which manifests as motion sickness and decrements in spatial orientation, postural control and locomotion, and manual and fine motor control. The risk of impairment is greatest during and soon after G-transitions when performance decrements may have high operational impact [manual landings, immediate egress following landing, early extravehicular activities (EVAs)]. The possible alterations in sensorimotor performance are of interest for lunar and Mars missions due to the prolonged microgravity exposure during transit followed by landing tasks. Gaps in knowledge include manual control ability around G-transitions, incidence, and severity of motion sickness during water landings, ability to perform EVAs soon after G-transition, and the effect of partial gravity. Current and future work on countermeasures includes sensorimotor training, self-administered rehabilitation, sensory augmentation, and in-flight balance training. Artificial gravity (centrifuge) would prevent multisensory integration changes and buy-down most risk. To characterize the long-term health effects of this risk, long term monitoring needs to be instated. Mitigation Strategy The mitigation strategy includes prevention, monitoring, and mitigation (treatment) of sensorimotor and neuro-vestibular disturbances induced by spaceflight that affect crew health and critical mission tasks. Operational countermeasures are being developed to address balance and locomotor deficits as well as motion sickness postlanding. This includes preflight and inflight training exercises, post-flight rehabilitation, sensory augmentation, and combining non-pharmacological countermeasures with new anti-motion sickness drug formulations. Sensorimotor assessments are being tied to exploration tasks to provide a quantitative index of readiness to perform key exploration tasks, as well as validating self-administered integrative countermeasure approaches suitable for autonomous exploration missions. HHC will also be addressing the risks associated with monitoring an automated landing and manually overriding the landing by characterizing post-flight piloting performance on a lunar landing motion-based simulation and testing countermeasures, such just-in-time on-orbit training, and using a perceptual modeling approach to enhance preflight simulations and inflight countermeasures.

title: Risk of Adverse Health Outcomes and Decrements in Performance Due to Medical Conditions that occur in Mission, as well as Long Term Health Outcomes Due to Mission Exposures
prompt: Explain NASA HRP Risk #95 (Medical Conditions): Risk of Adverse Health Outcomes and Decrements in Performance Due to Medical Conditions that occur in Mission, as well as Long Term Health Outcomes Due to Mission Exposures, its mission ratings, and clinical context.
response:
HRP Element: Exploration Medical Capability (ExMC). Risk Statement: Given that medical conditions will occur during human spaceflight missions, there is a possibility of adverse health outcomes & decrements in performance during these missions and for long term health. HSRB State of Knowledge Historical spaceflight data have revealed multiple in-flight and post flight medical conditions occur in the astronaut population. While none have led to loss of crew life, there have been three non-USOS in flight medical conditions leading to either evacuation or early termination of mission. The Integrated Medical Model provides evidence-based Probabilistic Risk Assessment (PRA) estimates for in-mission risk from 100 medical conditions modeled and is officially used for risk assessment after 2017 Transition to Operations. NASA has an occupational surveillance program that monitors long term health affects to astronauts due to spaceflight exposure. To date, minimal long term health impacts have been characterized from spaceflight exposure. The ability to predict an integrated long term health consequence is limited due to limited experience flying long duration crew members. Mitigation Strategy A human mission to Mars is a challenge outside of the bounds of human experience, but within the grasp of our technology and imagination. It is critical to both draw lessons from prior spaceflight experience and to recognize the limits of that experience. Each medical system designed for earlier human spaceflight was developed for a close-proximity, Earth-centered mission that enjoyed the advantages of real-time tele-medical support, consumable resupply, and medical evacuation when necessary. Operating outside low Earth orbit, without these advantages, requires a closer alignment between vehicle engineering and medical system development. In a real sense, success in a human Mars mission will depend on a comprehensive and mission-enabling astronaut healthcare system as well as an understanding of how such a system will be integrated and implemented within an exploration mission. All other design requirements and research within exploration medicine will be driven by the above goals; thus, these goals form the conceptual cornerstone that defines the medical system design and the supporting research pathway. Using this framework, the ExMC Element works to envision the medical needs for lunar/Artemis and Mars missions, to identify operational barriers to meeting those needs, and to implement a research pathway in the support of stakeholder needs and interests. The medical challenges expected in a Mars mission are unlike any prior human spaceflight experience. As a result, provision of medical care within the limitations of such a mission requires a paradigm shift in the understanding and acceptance of risk, the ethical framework of exploration missions, and the trading of medical capabilities against other vehicle components within a vehicle architecture limited by mass, volume, power, data, and many other factors unique to long-distance spaceflight. Medical system requirements and vehicle design must be integrated to minimize the risks to crews, and flexible and minimized technologies must factor heavily in system design to elevate a medical capability without sacrificing other systems components. It is imperative that the medical system balance these constraints to ensure that crew health and performance is maintained and mission risks are minimized. The ExMC Element is specifically concerned with establishing evidenced-based methods of monitoring and maintaining astronaut health. Essential to completing this task is the advancement in techniques that identify, prevent, and treat health threats that may occur during space missions. These techniques, in turn, must be supported by an evidence-based medical data architecture appropriate for long-duration, exploration-class missions. This exploration medical system will need to be designed for use in progressively Earth Independent Medical Operations (EIMO) , so that astronauts can function autonomously to maintain their own crew health and performance. ExMC is applying systems engineering principles and practices to accomplish its integrative goals. The systems engineering activities apply a structured and disciplined technical approach to support development of a medical system addressing clinical, behavioral health, human factors, physiological performance, and task performance needs. The systems engineering activities also enable effective coordination and integration with exploration mission engineering, operational, and technology development efforts by communicating with products (e.g., requirements, interface descriptions) typically used in those communities. Tools to support quantitative evaluation of medical risk, trade space analyses of clinical capabilities, development of technical requirements, and system implementation options will be necessary. Importantly, the medical system is just one component of a larger Crew Health and Performance (CHP) system and must integrate with other CHP systems, including Wellness, Task Performance, and Environmental Monitoring. This effort is intended to meet TH-8LM in NASA's 2022 Moon to Mars Objectives (hyperlink to this site https://www.nasa.gov/sites/default/files/atoms/files/m2m-objectives-exec-summary.pdf).

title: Risk of Radiation Carcinogenesis
prompt: Explain NASA HRP Risk #96 (Carcinogenesis): Risk of Radiation Carcinogenesis, its mission ratings, and clinical context.
response:
HRP Element: Space Radiation (SR). Risk Statement: LxC is the likelihood and consequence rating. The information above was last approved by the Human System Risk Board (HSRB) under the previous 3x4 LxC matrix. The HSRB has now migrated to a new 5x5 LxC matrix as defined in the new Risk Management Plan which may change the risk rating once brought forward for approval. This risk is scheduled to be updated at the 2025 HSRB. Given crew is exposed to radiation from the space environment, there is the possibility for increased cancer morbidity or mortality. HSRB State of Knowledge While epidemiological studies of terrestrial radiation-exposed cohorts demonstrate dose-related increases in cancer incidence and mortality at space relevant doses, no epidemiological data exists for exposures to space radiation. The space radiation environment differs from that present on Earth (e.g. x- and gamma-rays) due to the presence of high-energy particles including protons, heavy ions, and neutrons. Particles produce densely ionizing tracks and impart clustered damage difficult for cells to repair and current animal and cellular research suggests damage induced by particle radiation could increase cancer-related effects compared to x- or gamma-rays (i.e. reduced latency, increased malignancy). The NASA Space Cancer Risk (NSCR) model uses an established framework to estimate lifetime cancer risk from radiation exposure as the risk of exposure-induced death (REID). Human cancer epidemiology data from terrestrial radiation exposures are the basis for the model and a quality factor function is defined to transfer terrestrial radiation to the space environment. The current quality factor function is indirectly approximated using tumor endpoints from animal experiments and cancer-related endpoints from cellular experiments. Monte Carlo simulation techniques are used to incorporate uncertainties including radiation quality, dose and dose rate effects, terrestrial epidemiology models, and background population statistics and cancer rates. Uncertainty distributions can be updated as new relevant data becomes available. No validated medical countermeasures research to investigate biomedical countermeasures is ongoing in animals exposed to charged particles on the ground. Terrestrial cancer therapies continue to progress and may be able to mitigate cancer outcomes. Overall REID uncertainty is large with upper 95% confidence levels 3-4 times larger than estimated central values. The effects of other sources of uncertainty that may modify radiation risk (e.g. secondary spaceflight hazards) are being characterized but cannot be estimated or integrated currently. Mitigation Strategy One of the many environmental hazards in space flight is exposure to chronic, low dose-rate high-energy particles that make up the space radiation environment. These exposures increase the likelihood of cancer morbidity and mortality to crew over their lifetimes. Due to lack of resource availability and constraints in spacecraft design, shielding crew from the high energy particles that comprise the space radiation environment (87% protons, 12% helium, 1% higher charge and energy [HZE] ions) remains imperfect, leaving crew members exposed to the space radiation field, particularly during deep space and interplanetary missions. While operational risk assessment for the astronaut population is currently limited to estimates of excess cancer mortality, to mitigate the risk of radiation carcinogenesis, the Space Radiation Element has implemented a multi-effort research strategy to reduce the risk of both astronaut mortality and morbidity from cancer. Ground-based analog studies conducted at the NASA Space Radiation Laboratory (NSRL) are used to better characterize the role of radiation quality and dose-rate in space radiation-induced carcinogenesis using monoenergetic single ion beams. However, recent commissioning of various GCR simulation beams allows the Space Radiation Element to direct research efforts to understand potential impacts of a mixed field exposure approximating the local space radiation environment encountered inside a spacecraft during space flight. The interaction of other space flight stressors in modifying the risk of radiation carcinogenesis will be investigated. The information gained through these ongoing and future ground-based studies will help to characterize the carcinogenic risk from space radiation exposures as well as inform uncertainties in risk estimates. The initiation and implementation of the NASA Specialized Center of Research (NSCOR) tasked groups to characterize the different mechanisms of radiation carcinogenesis specific to the tissue types hypothesized to be major contributors to overall cancer risk including lung, breast, colon, the blood and lymphatic system (leukemia and lymphoma), liver, and brain. These efforts have led to the development of tissue-specific research models to support the identification of tissue-specific risk factors as well as contribute necessary information to aid in the early detection of pre-malignant disease and health monitoring through the identification of biomarkers. New, data-driven computational models are under investigation to assess radiation carcinogenesis risk and translate ground-based radiation research results to astronauts. The baseline NASA radiation carcinogenesis risk model is primarily based on human epidemiological data from the Life Span Study of atomic bomb survivors (LSS). Other radiation exposed cohorts, including the collection of radiation worker cohorts that make up the Million Person Study (MPS), will be assessed and incorporated to inform risk of radiogenic cancers arising from exposures more similar to the astronaut population. Specifically, the National Council of Radiation Protection (NCRP) has been commissioned to examine the role of sex dependence on radiogenic cancer rates. To test this and other risk model assumptions (including transfer of risk across populations, use of average incidence and mortality rates for the U.S. population, role of attained age and age at exposure, and radiation quality and dose-rate effects) past, current, and future data will be assessed using advanced biostatistical and computational methods. Further, to more fully understand the uncertainties surrounding assessment of radiation carcinogenesis risk, ensemble modeling approaches are being explored. Advances in terrestrial cancer early detection and treatment modalities will be monitored utilizing the 2017 Potomac Institute report entitled “Projection of U.S. Cancer Mortality and Incidence Rates” as a baseline. Ongoing clinical trials and translational research in cancer prevention and treatment will continue to be monitored and supported where appropriate. Collaborative committees with federal and state agencies (NCI, NAIAD, CPRIT) and cancer related professional societies (American Association for Cancer Research, American Society of Therapeutic Radiation Oncology, Radiation Research Society, etc.), and other stakeholders will monitor advancements in early detection and treatment outcomes. These advances will be utilized to inform best clinical practices for monitoring astronaut health during their career and into retirement. Interagency collaboration will also help develop infrastructure to support identification and validation of medical countermeasures to reduce carcinogenesis risk in appropriate biological models. The Space Radiation Element will continue to sponsor studies utilizing a systems biology approach to provide a framework to integrate mechanistic studies of cancer risk across multiple levels of understanding (molecular, cellular, tissue, systems, and organismal levels). Limited informatics data sets (transcriptomics, genome sequencing, etc.), and the establishment of tissue archives will provide resources for future analysis to answer specific questions in a timely fashion. Tech watches and research surveys to explore new approaches in terrestrial cancer research and model development will also be implemented to leverage the broader field of cancer research to support tissue-specific risk assessment. Specific goals, deliverables, and recommended targets for closure efforts are outlined in the Cancer Gaps and questions can be directed to the Space Radiation Element Scientist, Deputy Element Scientist, and Discipline Leads.

title: Risk of Adverse Cognitive or Behavioral Changes and Psychiatric Disorders Leading to In-mission Health and Performance and Long-term Health Effects
prompt: Explain NASA HRP Risk #99 (Behavioral Health): Risk of Adverse Cognitive or Behavioral Changes and Psychiatric Disorders Leading to In-mission Health and Performance and Long-term Health Effects, its mission ratings, and clinical context.
response:
HRP Element: Human Factors and Behavioral Performance (HFBP). Risk Statement: Given that crews of future exploration missions will be exposed to extended duration of isolation and confinement, greater distances from Earth, as well as increased exposures to radiation and altered gravity, there is a possibility that these singular or combined hazards could lead to (a) adverse cognitive or behavioral changes affecting crew health and performance during the mission; (b) development of psychiatric disorders if adverse behavioral health changes are undetected or inadequately mitigated; and (c) long term health consequences, including late-emerging cognitive and behavioral changes. HSRB State of Knowledge Sub-diagnostic behavioral health conditions were anecdotally reported on several long-duration missions. Inflight symptoms have never reached diagnostic threshold despite related instances of lost mission objectives or early return. Estimated ISS incidence of behavioral health symptoms is 0.62 person-year, but is likely an underestimate. Incidence of psychiatric disorders in Antarctic ground analogs is ≥4.5%; increase in behavioral health symptoms over time with a preliminary non-linear increased incidence past 5-6 months has been found in experimental analogs. Brain morphology and functional alterations in long-duration ISS astronauts draw concern for cognitive performance or long-term health implications but are unknowns. Biomarker data reveal declines in a key neurotrophin linked to volumetric reductions in long-duration ground analogs. Case report and anecdotal evidence indicates inconsistent, mild cognitive decrements in LEO. Clinically meaningful cognitive decrements post-landing are hypothesized to relate to physiological adaptation and persisted at least 6 months post-landing in a single case study; lifetime course and prevalence are unknowns. Animal research suggests possible short-term cognitive decrements due to radiation with uncertain human translatability. Limited study of adult atomic bomb survivors indicates no excess neurodegenerative disease likelihood. Adult cranial radiotherapy survivors show clinically meaningful cognitive decrements from high-dose terrestrial radiation and some evidence of excess neurodegenerative disease likelihood. There is minimal-to-no evidence of excess neurodegenerative diseases in short-duration LEO astronauts; likelihood for long-duration and DRMs beyond LEO is unknown. Most current countermeasures have limited feasibility beyond LEO, increasing risk. Mitigation Strategy The risk mitigation strategy of the Human Factors and Behavioral Health (HFBP) Element follows the larger strategy of the HRP “from Evidence to Deliverables” principle, with the involvement of Medical and Mission Operations to help determine the mitigations that are relevant for current and future spaceflight. Specific tasks are defined to address the gaps and provide clear, specific deliverables for long duration spaceflight, ensuring an evidence and operationally-based end item. Based on scientific and operational evidence, HFBP systematically identifies the appropriate platform (e.g., laboratory, ground analog) to address the gaps prior to validating in spaceflight. To ensure relevancy, stakeholders are engaged in the process from the beginning. Evidence gathered from HFBP research characterizes Risk, informs Operations and Standards, and yields countermeasures for performance and behavioral health. HFBP research addresses the risk of adverse cognitive and behavioral conditions and psychiatric disorders developing during or following a long-duration mission. Early detection of stress, cognitive or behavioral changes from baseline, or other risk factors during spaceflight is imperative to deter development of cognitive or behavioral conditions or psychiatric disorders which could seriously harm and negatively impact the individual or the crew, and pose serious consequences for accomplishing mission objectives or jeopardizing the mission altogether. Toward this end, HFBP is developing methods for monitoring cognitive and behavioral health during a long-duration exploration mission, and adapting/refining various tools and technologies for use in the spaceflight environment. These measures and tools will be used to monitor, detect, and treat early risk factors. HFBP will utilize analogs to test, further refine, and validate these measures and tools for future missions. HFBP also develops countermeasures for maintaining cognitive and behavioral health and enhancing performance during long-duration isolated, confined, and highly autonomous missions; provides recommendations regarding space medicine best practices; and, provides updates for behavioral health and performance standards. Integrated Research Approach Spaceflight stressors are experienced simultaneously, thus cognitice and behavioral changes can be induced by many spaceflight factors. To that end, HFBP developed a fully integrated research plan to address three high-priority risk factors impacting crew health and performance and are believed to be synergistically related: space radiation, isolation, and altered gravity exposure on long-duration missions. The "Risk of Acute (In-flight) and Late Central Nervous System Effects from Radiation Exposure" is now embedded within the BMed Risk, and hence relevant efforts from the combined BMed Risk and the Sensorimotor Risk ("Risk of Impaired Control of Spacecraft/Associated Systems and Decreased Mobility Due to Vestibular/Sensorimotor Alterations Associated with Spaceflight (SM)" were combined into an integrated approach referred to as the CNS/BMed/Sensorimotor (CBS) Integrated Research Plan. The BMed risk has been designated as the "parent risk" for the CBS Integrated Research Plan. NASA seeks to accelerate research advances and scientific progress with this integrated research approach to assess and characterize the combined effects of spaceflight hazards related to crew health and performance. Since spaceflight hazards impinge and act upon the human system (the crew), there is an increasing recognition of the importance of characterizing the risks in a completely integrated manner with transdisciplinary expertise. With long-duration crew exposed to multiple risks, NASA is seeking research to understand, analyze and quantify the risk from simultaneous exposure to multiple spaceflight environmental factors potentially impacting crew health and performance. For example, given that the behavioral medicine (BMed) risk focuses on changes to cognitive functioning, there is a need to characterize the potential interactive or synergistic risk (cf., Greco et al., 1995) to crew health and performance when isolated and confined while simultaneously exposed to space radiation. The potential impact of inflight CNS alterations and sensorimotor (SM) adaptations that may alter brain structure and function must also be understood (Koppelsmans et al., 2017; Mao et al., 2016; Pulga, Porte, Morel, 2016). Evidence indicates that many spaceflight stressors, including altered gravity, sleep loss, radiation exposure, and isolation and confinement, may all lead to dysregulation of the brain's structure and microenvironment, leading to imbalanced function of neuronal and glial networks and the neurovascular unit (Cassady et al., 2016; Van Ombergen et al., 2017). The magnitude of physical and biological stressors will vary by mission phases but will simultaneously, perhaps synergistically, and cumulatively act on the human system with the potential to adversely impact operationally-relevant crew performance. This suggests the need to identify the types and magnitude of interactions as they affect behavior, especially as it relates to operationally significant performance (e.g., performance that depends on reaction time, situational vigilance, and memory of complex procedures). Complementing cognitive and behavioral performance measures, this CBS Integrated Research Plan identifies a need to assess brain physiology, neurovascular unit integrity, molecular signaling, and biomarker changes, in order to generate data sets that can be incorporated into computational models (see e.g., Muldoon et al., 2016) to represent and predict changes in operationally-relevant "brain performance pathways". HFBP's conceptualization of Brain Performance Pathways (BPP) is based on how the architecture of brain networks at rest guide the connectivity patterns that emerge during the performance of various tasks (i.e. modularity measured during "resting states" predicts working memory performance and stimulus detection in a perceptual task) (see e.g., Bassett et al., 2011; Cassady et al., 2016; Dosenbach et al., 2007; Fair et al., 2009; Fox et al., 2007; Meunier et al., 2009; van den Heuvel et al., 2009). Relating this finding to operationally-relevant performance is research evidence that demonstrates those scoring higher on IQ tests show smaller functional connectivity changes between "resting state" and "task performance states" (suggesting more efficient adaptation to task demands). Thus, specific impacts on brain focal regions (see e.g., Boes et al., 2015) are important for us to understand since cortical organization reveals a "between-module connectivity" that when disrupted, is associated with widespread cognitive dysfunction (and spaceflight is associated with activating a cortical re-organization, see e.g., Demertzi et al., 2016; and in simulated microgravity, Pani et al., 2013). In addition, given the different sensitivities of brain tissue to both qualities and quantities (doses) of radiation, stress, and altered gravity, there is a recognized need to conceptualize and assess the functionality and stability of the connectivity patterns, as representative of BPPs. Further, it is unknown to what extent these differential vulnerabilities are due to alterations in modular networks. This suggests a need to determine how a more modular brain network may potentiate countermeasure (CM) action (e.g., up-regulation of neurotrophic factors have been associated with exercise-induced changes in brain connectivity) (Rajab et al., 2014). This underscores the importance of conceptualizing BPPs and the role of a modular structure in enabling brain processes that support a wide range of operationally-relevant performance and behaviors. This conceptualization also allows for consideration of the putative role of "Cognitive Reserve" and the potential for a measure of cortical organization to serve as a "biomarker" for that capability (Clewett et al., 2016). Past CNS research with radiation has shown that various outcome measures exhibit differential radiation sensitivities, which may in turn reflect differential sensitivity of underlying BPPs (see e.g., NASA CNS Risk Evidence Report, 2016). Thus, there is need to characterize whether there are synergistic or interactive impacts of stressors on CBS risks by conceptualizing and assessing impacts to operationally-relevant “brain performance pathways” comprised of the neural circuitry and associated molecular, cellular and physiological processes that underlie specific behaviors or sets of behaviors expressed in animal models that are translatable to human performance (Elmer et al., 2016). In addition, remarkable research within the radiation biology community has identified synaptic and neurophysiological changes that have increased our understanding of the functional properties of microcircuit alterations associated with decrements in relevant behavioral performance paradigms (see e.g., Parihar et al., 2014, Rudobeck et al., 2017, Rabin et al., 2011, Britten et al., 2018, NASA CNS Risk Evidence Report, 2016). While these changes in neurophysiology and performance yield translatable insights into specific cognitive operations and modeling for single sites, there is a need to conceptually bridge the alterations in neurophysiology and circuity mechanisms that give rise to the observed biological signals and changes in performance to identify BPPs nodes related to both BMed and SM operationally-relevant performance (NASA CNS Risk Evidence Report, 2016). The CBS research integration is intended to help NASA accelerate our research efforts to characterize the relevant operational performance risks posed by space radiation exposure, isolation and confinement, and altered gravity. There is a recognition that the complete, transdisciplinary integration of the three specialized scientific fields will enhance creativity and accelerate discovery as we apply the unique expertise to the scientific problems, integrate our efforts, and share our ideas in order to generate fundamentally new conceptual frameworks and methodological approaches. This transdisciplinary, integrative approach is intended to transcend scientific disciplinary origins to deliver standards, guidelines and countermeasures responsive to space exploration needs. The CBS Integrated Research Plan completely integrates scientific expertise within the 3 discipline areas (space radiation, sensorimotor and behavioral health) to operationalize a risk-assessment approach in order to define crew health and performance related to: 1. Operational performance and fitness for duty standards relative to each risk within the framework of Performance Outcome Levels (POL). 2. Radiation Permissible Exposure Limits (PEL) (established by assessing the relative risks of the CBS Integrated Risks). Deliverables: Standards development (which includes POLs and PELs) requires complementary, translational approaches to identify the mechanisms, pathways, and components that contribute to operational performance risks by: Appreciation of multifactorial nature of spaceflight hazards, exposures, & dose-effect responses (i.e. differential variability due to differences in vulnerability to hazards). Consistent/valid animal translational models (and back-translational approaches), along with human biomarkers and measures to assess the function of some mechanisms discovered in animal models, used to develop a multidimensional set of validity criteria that is then generalized to relevant human risk. Leveraging translational and computational modeling to integrate traditional and novel data (e.g., animal model analogues of brain-behavior risk translated to human performance). title: Risk of Performance Decrements and Adverse Health Outcomes Resulting from Sleep Loss, Circadian Desynchronization, and Work Overload

HRP Element: Human Factors and Behavioral Performance (HFBP). Risk Statement: Given that astronauts experience sleep loss, circadian desynchronization, and work overload, there is a possibility that performance decrements and adverse health outcomes will occur. HSRB State of Knowledge There is evidence of sleep deficiency inflight as crews sleep 6 h/night and increase their sleep and circadian misalignment. There is also evidence of work overload and scheduling issues. Ground studies demonstrate that despite perception that one can adapt, these risk factors cause short-term performance, mood, psychosocial, and metabolic decrements and are associated with long term poor health outcomes including increased risk of Alzheimer's Disease, cardiovascular disease, hormone-dependent cancer, and diabetes. Specific tasks are defined to address the gaps and provide clear, specific deliverables for long duration spaceflight, ensuring an evidence and operationally-based end item. Working with research and operational experts, HFBP systematically identifies the appropriate platform to address the gaps prior to validating in spaceflight. To ensure relevancy, stakeholders are engaged in the process from the beginning. Evidence gathered from HFBP research characterize Risk, inform Operations and Standards, and yield countermeasures for performance and behavioral health. title: Risk of In-Mission Performance and Behavioral Health Decrements Due to Inadequate Cooperation, Coordination, Communication, and Psychosocial Adaptation within a Team
prompt: Explain NASA HRP Risk #101 (Team): Risk of In-Mission Performance and Behavioral Health Decrements Due to Inadequate Cooperation, Coordination, Communication, and Psychosocial Adaptation within a Team, its mission ratings, and clinical context.
response:
HRP Element: Human Factors and Behavioral Performance (HFBP). Risk Statement: Given that the conditions of space missions may lead to inadequate functioning within a team (inadequate cooperation, coordination, communication and/or psychosocial adaptation), which includes flight crew and ground support, there is a possibility that performance and behavioral health decrements will occur. HSRB State of Knowledge There is evidence of occasional conflict within crews preflight and in-flight, within and across International Space Station (ISS) partner subgroups. ISS crews reported concerns with crew readiness to engage in effective teamwork during off-nominal events. In off-nominal events identified as requiring "exceptional" teamwork, crews have responded incorrectly. There is evidence of significant impacts on individual and team performance, stress, and cohesion caused by communication delays and coordination inefficiencies between crew and the Mission Control Center (MCC). There is evidence of occasional team preparedness deficiencies during preflight and in-flight due to switching between individual and team activities, and team and technical skill decay. Selection has successfully incorporated individual-level assessments of team skills and capabilities, but crew composition is not data-driven. Team training and performance is not systematically monitored nor evaluated, except confidentially by operational psychologists. Commercialization and private astronaut crew integration with professional astronauts introduce risk to NASA astronauts, but the level or risk is not well-quantified. Mitigation Strategy The risk mitigation strategy of the HFBP Element follows the larger strategy of the HRP “from Evidence to Products” principle, while being driven by Operations. Specific tasks are defined to address the gaps and provide clear, specific deliverables, ensuring an evidence- and operationally-based end item. To ensure relevancy, stakeholders are engaged in the process at the beginning. Findings from HFBP research inform operations, standards, and updates to the evidence base for the HFBP Risks. The mitigation strategy for this area of research is to develop an empirically-based approach to identify the most relevant and serious threats to task performance, teamwork, and psycho-social performance within the team context. Utilizing a common set of criteria will allow for the systematic review and analysis of knowledge as well as current practices/policies when implementing Behavioral Health and Performance (BHP) operations. Once these threats have been identified, researchers will determine the most effective ways to monitor and measure these threats as well as identify the optimal and timely countermeasures to mitigate risk. Countermeasures integrate individual- and team-level psychological processes with human factors design relative to habitability, training, and interactions with robotics, computers, and automated systems to manage risk from multiple perspectives. Notably, specific factors have been identified as highly relevant to long-duration space missions (e.g., crew composition, communication, autonomy, team skills). Thus, these gaps will focus specifically on understanding the true impact of these factors on long duration missions and mitigating the risk through countermeasure development.

title: Risk of Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS)
prompt: Explain NASA HRP Risk #105 (SANS): Risk of Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS), its mission ratings, and clinical context.
response:
HRP Element: Human Health Countermeasures (HHC). Risk Statement: Given that ocular and brain structural changes develop during spaceflight, there is a possibility that these changes could lead to short-term or long-term vision alterations, cognitive effects, or other deleterious health effects. HSRB State of Knowledge Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS) is a syndrome unique to humans that fly in space, and there is no terrestrial disease equivalent. Data collected pre-, in-, and post-flight indicate that 70% of crewmembers experience one or more of the hallmark signs of SANS: optic disc edema, chorioretinal folds, globe flattening, or hyperopic shifts in refractive error. Major SANS knowledge gaps include: underlying mechanism(s), including role of intracranial pressure (ICP) and factors contributing to individual variability of presentation; threshold where physiological adaptations transition to pathology; proven countermeasures; and long-term health consequences. The effect of spaceflight on brain structure is being investigated, but an association between SANS and brain structure or function (cognition) has not been established. Mitigation Strategy The Human Research Program (HRP) is dedicated to discovering the best methods and technologies to determine the cause and contributing factors to SANS, as well as developing strategies and countermeasures to prevent or mitigate SANS. Space Medicine Operations manages the risk from a clinical perspective. Since 2009, medical surveillance has expanded and includes comprehensive pre-, in-, and postflight assessment of ocular parameters, including optical coherence tomography (OCT) images, ocular ultrasound, ophthalmic imaging, and visual acuity testing. Visual Fields testing occurs before and immediately after spaceflight, and long-term follow up occurs approximately ~every 3 years. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and eyes occurs before flight and within the first 3 days after return to Earth. Ultimately, the goal of both Space Medicine Operations and HRP is to identify and implement a set of preventative and/or countermeasures for SANS. There is a multifaceted research approach that aims to determine the underlying risk factors for developing SANS, to test possible countermeasures to prevent or reverse it, and to identify potential long-term health outcomes resulting from SANS findings. Findings from this research will be used to inform mitigation strategies. Research is currently being conducted through retrospective data sharing to conduct advanced novel quantitative analyses and identify correlations among the SANS signs and symptoms. Studies also include use of modeling to help inform the SANS etiology. Moreover, prospective research studies are being conducted to characterize SANS, which include determining the role of the cephalad fluid shift, identifying potential visual functional changes, tied to the ocular structural findings, investigations to determine relationships between the documented ocular and brain structure changes, and investigating potential genetic or anatomical predisposition to developing SANS. Recently, research findings have provided evidence that the earliest signs of optic disc edema can be detected based on an increase in total retinal thickness measured from optical coherence tomography images. These data suggest ~70% of crew flying 4-6 month long missions to the International Space Station develop early signs of optic disc edema. Technology currently on ISS to address SANS includes visual acuity testing software, ocular ultrasound, ophthalmic imaging, and optical coherence tomography, including OCT MulitColor Imaging. In addition, research studies include preflight and postflight MRI of the brain and eye. Additional research will focus on following astronauts after return from long-duration ISS missions to determine if any long term visual function deficits develop. Use of strict head-down tilt bed rest as a ground-based analog of SANS was first established in 2017 and has been used to test potential countermeasures since 2018, including ongoing studies expected to be completed in 2023. In addition, parabolic flight studies have been used to characterize acute cephalad venous fluid shifts, while the use of a spectrum of gravitational levels to understand if surface operations on the Moon or Mars may reverse the headward fluid shift that occurs in weightlessness will occur in 2023. Future flight studies are being planned to test candidate countermeasures in crewmembers flying long-duration missions to the ISS. Studies to determine the long-term health consequences, including eye and brain structure and function are currently in the definition phase. Data obtained from these studies will enable closure of these gaps and facilitate SANS countermeasure development. Medical Standards and Clinical Practice Guidelines are used by Space Medicine Operations to protect the safety of the crew, and as research progresses, findings will be transferred to Operations.

title: Risk of In-Mission Injury and Performance Decrements and Long-term Health Effects due to Dynamic Loads
prompt: Explain NASA HRP Risk #167 (Dynamic Loads): Risk of In-Mission Injury and Performance Decrements and Long-term Health Effects due to Dynamic Loads, its mission ratings, and clinical context.
response:
HRP Element: Human Factors and Behavioral Performance (HFBP). Risk Statement: Given the exposure to the range of anticipated dynamic loads that might be applied to crew within the hostile closed environment of a spacecraft and/or surface vehicle (suited or unsuited) could result in injury to the crew, resulting in a possibility that mission task performance would be impaired, or tasks could not be performed. HSRB State of Knowledge Standards and vehicle design requirements are based on automotive and military environments and operational protocols; they are also partially tailored to the spaceflight environment. However, these do not adequately mitigate the risk of injury due to the unique spaceflight environment. Current analytical tools are used outside of their validation conditions and have been shown to under predict Soyuz landing injury. Injury due to standing during dynamic phases of flight is poorly documented in the literature and little data are available. Injury assessment reference values have not been validated due to limited load and injury data from Soyuz landings. Mitigation Strategy The Occupant Protection Team at NASA has developed a forward plan to develop new standards for protecting the crew during dynamic phases of flight. In collaboration with external peers in industry, academia, and other government agencies, the Team will develop and validate the standards using a combination of data mining, testing, analysis, simulation, and expert opinion. Because all crewmembers must endure dynamic phases of flight, detailed understanding of the human body response to such environments is critical. In addition, because spaceflight-deconditioning causes decreases in bone strength, decreases in muscle strength, and increases in bone fracture risk, the criticality of this understanding is greater with longer duration spaceflight missions.

title: Risk of Mission Impacts and Long-Term Health Issues due to Decompression Sickness
prompt: Explain NASA HRP Risk #168 (DCS): Risk of Mission Impacts and Long-Term Health Issues due to Decompression Sickness, its mission ratings, and clinical context.
response:
HRP Element: Human Health Countermeasures (HHC). Risk Statement: Given that decompression sickness (DCS) is a potential risk for every spaceflight/mission (e.g., EVA or cabin depressurization) and must be mitigated to acceptable risk levels; limitations in quantitative understanding of DCS will lead to conservative DCS risk mitigation countermeasures with significant operational, engineering, and/or secondary health/performance impacts. HSRB State of Knowledge As of today, no reported cases of DCS during flight, yet ground studies with similar decompression stress do cause DCS. Ground studies stop at first symptoms of DCS, so little is known on the progression of DCS symptoms. NASA standards exist for both DCS prevention and treatment and are being incorporated into new programs. Effects of fractional gravity on DCS risk are currently unknown, but will increase the risk compared to microgravity. Current operational pre-breathe (PB) protocols are validated only for the microgravity environment and require hours of PB including multiple procedural steps requiring ground and intravehicular (IV) support to facilitate timing and order of airlock and suit preparation operations. Countermeasure Development: Based on a successful staged decompression to a 10.2 psia / 26.5% O2 atmosphere developed for shuttle EVA to reduce prep. time. The 8.2 psia / 34% O2 environment with variable pressure space suit is the recommended approach and is being validated to support an efficient and flexible EVA architecture, however, the ability to implement the Exploration Atmosphere as recommended may be affected by factors including: schedule & budgetary constraints, contract mechanisms, international partnerships, personnel changes, cross-program dependencies, and unanticipated technical challenges. Ability to accurately inform major cross-program architectural decisions is limited by significant uncertainty in unvalidated DCS risk estimation tools. Mitigation Strategy Research tasks associated with understanding, quantifying, and mitigating the risk of DCS during spaceflight are described in the EVA Risk Strategy ( https://humanresearchroadmap.nasa.gov/risks/risk.aspx?i=84 ).

title: Risk of Reduced Crew Health and Performance Due to Hypoxia
prompt: Explain NASA HRP Risk #173 (Hypoxia): Risk of Reduced Crew Health and Performance Due to Hypoxia, its mission ratings, and clinical context.
response:
HRP Element: Human Health Countermeasures (HHC). Risk Statement: Given that future human exploration missions require robust, flexible Extravehicular Activity (EVA) architecture protocols that include the use of a reduced pressure cabin atmosphere enabling staged denitrogenation, there is a possibility that this atmosphere could result in compromised health and performance to the crewmember due to exposure to mild hypobaric hypoxia. Notes: - In addition to hypobaric hypoxia associated with staged denitrogenation, there are additional factors that can result in hypoxic exposure to the crewmember such as cabin depressurization, Environmental Control and Life Support System (ECLSS) failure, toxic exposure or crewmember illness/injury. - Planned research and countermeasures will focus on mild hypoxia associated with hypoxia related to staged denitrogenation. HSRB State of Knowledge The exploration atmosphere (8.2 psia/34% O2) was selected by the Exploration Atmospheres Working Group (EAWG) because it was considered to be a mildly hypoxic atmosphere with acceptable flammability risk and low O2 prebreathe (PB) overhead to maintain acceptable DCS risk while facilitating efficient EVA operations. The 8.2/34 environment (PI O2 = 128 mmHg) is physiologically similar in terms of O2 availability to the nominal shuttle and ISS staged decompression atmosphere of 10.2 psia / 26.5% O2 (PI O2 = 127 mmHg). Both environments provide a hypoxic dose as modeled between 4000-8300 ft altitude. The staged decompression was used on 40 different shuttle missions for durations of 1 to 8 days. Of most concern are the potential effects on the increased intracranial pressure, visual impairment, cognitive performance, sensorimotor dysfunction, oxidative damage and sleep quality. Other areas of focus include incidence and treatment of acute mountain sickness (AMS), development of new exercise countermeasure protocols and effective food preparation at 8.2 psia. Per HLS requirements, the original 7-day limit in NASA-STD-3001 for mildly hypoxic environments was extended to 30 days with monitoring because it was shown to improve the net risk posture for flight crew health and performance. With an agreement on what monitoring is required, this 30-day duration could be extended to indefinite with monitoring for all missions other than Mars, which will need additional assessment due to the long transit in microgravity prior to use of staged denitrogenation environments. Mitigation Strategy Research tasks to investigate physiological responses and mitigating hypoxia risk associated with exposure to hypobaric hypoxic stress as an exploration atmosphere and cycling between mild hypoxia and mild hyperoxia during EVAs is captured under the EVA Risk Strategy ( https://humanresearchroadmap.nasa.gov/risks/risk.aspx?i=84 ).

title: Risk of Adverse Mission Outcomes Due to Earth Independent Human-Systems Operations
prompt: Explain NASA HRP Risk #175 (EIHSO): Risk of Adverse Mission Outcomes Due to Earth Independent Human-Systems Operations, its mission ratings, and clinical context.
response:
HRP Element: Human Factors and Behavioral Performance (HFBP). Risk Statement: Given decreasing real-time ground support for execution of Earth independent critical, complex operations during future exploration missions, there is a possibility of adverse performance outcomes, most consequentially that crew are unable to adequately respond to unanticipated critical malfunctions or execute safety-critical procedures. HSRB State of Knowledge Critical malfunctions requiring Crew/Mission Control Center (MCC) management occurred at a rate of 1.7 times per year for International Space Station (ISS) averaged over the lifetime and 3-4 times per year in the burn in phase for the vehicle. These averages do not include EVA data, which greatly increases the incident rate. Prior experience from the Apollo program showed 10/11 crewed missions experienced significant anomalies where crew relied heavily on MCC expertise in real-time. These failure patterns are in line with those observed in other complex engineered systems (e.g., oil rigs, launch systems, commercial aviation, etc.). Mitigation Strategy The Human Systems Integration Architecture (HSIA) risk is comprised of an integrated representation of the Human Factors risk areas of vehicle design and habitability, human computer interaction, human automation and robotics integration, training, and task design. Future deep space missions will present new challenges for crew, and increased risks to human performance due to the stress, fatigue, radiation exposure, and isolation that characterizes these missions. In addition, crew will no longer be able to depend on real-time support from Mission Control due to distance from the Earth, but will have to work increasingly autonomously, performing critical tasks that were previously carried out by Flight Controllers. This greater crew/vehicle autonomy will depend, in part on advanced, on-board automated systems but also on new approaches to training, teaming and crew selection. Most importantly, it will depend on a successful integration of intelligent vehicle capabilities with crew capabilities. Ground laboratories, analogs, and the International Space Station (ISS) are utilized to answer research questions necessary to ensure that future Exploration crewmembers, who will be dealing with many unknowns, communication delays, and increasing autonomy, will be able to adequately perform their tasks and complete their missions. The HSIA risk provides a conceptual framework proposed to address the integration of onboard capability and crew roles and responsibilities necessary to enable crew to respond effectively and efficiently in the required increasing autonomous mission operations framework. Enabling a flight crew of 4 to perform the job that has traditionally been done by a ground crew of 40+ will require a fundamental rethinking of crew-vehicle integration and operations as well as crew-ground collaboration. A flight crew of 4 will need to function more autonomously in response to anticipated reduction in communication quantity and quality as well as unanticipated blackouts instead of depending on frequent real-time communications with a large Mission Control Center (MCC) ground support team of diverse specialties to provide directions (see Dempsey et al., 2018 for a detailed description of the range of support MCC provides). As outlined by Vera and Wu (2018), the impact will be felt particularly in dealing with unanticipated, off-nominal situations. Our current operational models therefore (tied to ground control) must evolve as mission operations become increasingly earth independent. Decreasing real-time ground support for the execution of complex operations during future exploration missions will require the flight crew to respond to potentially safety-critical anomalies with no established procedures on their own. A delay or absence of ground support during unanticipated contingencies can become a significant hazard and increase the risk of jeopardizing crew and vehicle safety if there are not sufficient onboard capabilities to assist with troubleshooting and contingency management. The attainment of increased crew autonomy therefore lies in the ability to complement and enhance crew capabilities so that the 4-person flight crew can, on their own, perform the kind of anomaly response that had previously been done mostly by MCC, and complete these activities in the face of the expected communication delays or unexpected blackouts. It is important to highlight that complex, engineered systems, automated/autonomous or not, will experience unanticipated safety critical malfunctions. These can be due, in part or in whole, to human error and/or space environment impacts, but can also be independent of these. Humans are the critical problem-solving components of complex engineered systems and while Artificial Intelligence, Intelligent/Autonomous Systems can help the human decision maker, especially with pattern analysis, the AI systems will not be able to provide actual problem-solving. Furthermore, reducing the number of crew in any system has the potential to raise risks of non-optimal Human System Integration in unanticipated ways. It is therefore critical that c apabilities be wrapped around the human(s) in order for safety critical issues to be addressable. To further mitigate the risk, specific factors have been identified (e.g., autonomy, anomaly detection and response, etc.) as highly relevant to long duration space missions. Thus, these gaps will focus specifically on understanding the true impact of these factors on long duration missions. At the conclusion of each task, the final report is reviewed and the relevant evidence report is modified or updated to indicate how the results of the research or technology activity address the gaps and contribute to quantifying or mitigating risk or risks. If applicable, the results will also be incorporated into NASA-STD-3001, VOL. II and the Human Integration Design Handbook (HIDH). Evaluations of countermeasure strategies will be made available in the evidence base and recommendations specific to countermeasure implementation for future missions, will also be defined.
