title: Risk of Performance Decrement and Crew Illness Due to Inadequate Food and Nutrition
prompt: Explain NASA HRP Risk #176 (Food and Nutrition): Risk of Performance Decrement and Crew Illness Due to Inadequate Food and Nutrition, its mission ratings, and clinical context.
response:
HRP Element: Human Health Countermeasures (HHC). Risk Statement: Given that there is a constrained ability to supply adequate food in spaceflight missions, there is a possibility that inadequate nutrition will result in performance decrement, crew illness, and long-term health effects. HSRB State of Knowledge Much is known about the basic nutrition required to maintain performance and health during spaceflight. Standards/controls exist to maintain food safety during spaceflight. Ground data indicates that dehydration and "quicker than usual" weight loss in physically fit individuals will impact cognition and performance. Adequate nutrition and safe food have been demonstrated for 6-month missions and limited 1-year missions that have resupply. Optimizing food/nutrient intake will likely benefit multiple systems, will drive nutrient requirement definitions, and food provisions. There is an uncharacterized risk during LO and LOS missions due to resource restrictions and increased EVAs resulting in reduced food provisioning and preparation capability compared to ISS. The capability to provide safe pre-packaged food with a 5-year shelf life that provides adequate nutrition content, acceptability, safety and variety is a gap. Some countermeasures (CMs) being investigated are: Bioregenerative supplementation and alternative processing, packaging and storage. The impact of both the current and proposed exploration food systems on cognition, performance, behavior, and many other aspects of health is not adequately understood. Potential health impacts include 1) reductions in crew performance (loss of endurance, cognition); 2) crew illness (loss of bone and muscle mass, immune function, cardiovascular performance, gastrointestinal function, severe dehydration, nausea, diarrhea, endocrine function, ocular, psychological health, and the ability to mitigate oxidative damage); 3) long term health effects (cancer, bone, cardio, etc.), 4) interactions with other systems/countermeasures (e.g., drug/nutrient interactions, environment influences on oxidative stress, exercise-induced alterations in energy reqs.). Mitigation Strategy To develop requirements for a nutritious, acceptable/palatable, and safe food system that in addition to providing sustenance can act as a physiological and psychological countermeasure while being balanced with resource constraints.

title: Risk of Ineffective or Toxic Medications During Long-Duration Exploration Spaceflight
prompt: Explain NASA HRP Risk #177 (Pharm): Risk of Ineffective or Toxic Medications During Long-Duration Exploration Spaceflight, its mission ratings, and clinical context.
response:
HRP Element: Exploration Medical Capability (ExMC). Risk Statement: Given that there is no current method to sufficiently characterize medication use, drug quality and performance, clinical outcomes, and the impact of a hostile space environment on pharmaceutical stability and potency during long-duration exploration missions, there is a possibility that provision of a safe and effective drug treatment will be significantly limited, impacting crew health and performance. HSRB State of Knowledge FDA standards followed for Low Earth Orbit (LEO) – require frequent up mass (yearly), which will be problematic for some long duration missions and impossible for Mars Preparatory and Planetary DRMs. Effects of spaceflight environmental conditions on medication stability for long-duration and deep space missions are not fully characterized. It is unclear of how, and to what extent, the spaceflight environment and resultant alterations of human physiology may affect drug pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties. The potential for drug instability compounded by altered drug response poses a significant risk to exploration crews. Additionally, engineering has concerns about medication/suit compatibility. This affects what medications can be administered to the crew in suited operations. The Human Research Program Element (ExMC) research efforts are underway to propose a safe and effective exploration spaceflight formulary able to maintain a ≥ 3 year shelf-life. The proposed ExMC strategy will provide validation for the chemical / physical pharmaceutical stability, degradation product toxicity, and drug safety profiles, and better characterize pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, and pharmacotherapeutic properties of drugs in the exploration spaceflight environment. Mitigation Strategy NASA’s current Low Earth Orbit (LEO) operations involve frequent resupply missions that may be problematic for some long duration missions and impossible for deep space exploration missions. As such, ensuring a safe and effective pharmacy for exploration missions is an important challenge. At this time, it is unclear how, and to what extent, 1) the spaceflight environment changes drug stability and 2) alterations of human physiology or the medications themselves affect drug pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties. The potential for drug instability compounded by altered drug response may pose a risk to exploration crews. Current research efforts are underway to propose a safe and effective exploration spaceflight formulary able to maintain a ≥ 3 year shelf-life. The proposed ExMC research includes: analysis of medication packaging and storage solutions; studies that will provide validation for chemical / physical pharmaceutical stability; degradation product toxicity and drug safety profiles; and better characterize pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, and pharmacotherapeutic properties of medications in spaceflight.

title: Risk of Cardiovascular Adaptations Contributing to Adverse Mission Performance and Health Outcomes
prompt: Explain NASA HRP Risk #179 (Cardiovascular): Risk of Cardiovascular Adaptations Contributing to Adverse Mission Performance and Health Outcomes, its mission ratings, and clinical context.
response:
HRP Element: Human Health Countermeasures (HHC). Risk Statement: Given exposure to the spaceflight environment can contribute to cardiovascular deconditioning, dysfunction, and remodeling, there is a possibility that crews will experience impaired performance and adverse cardiovascular health outcomes that necessitate intervention during and after spaceflight and planetary operations. HSRB State of Knowledge Exposure to weightlessness and the resulting headward fluid shift alters blood volume, flow, and pressure, manifesting in changes in vascular and cardiac structure and function (e.g., cardiovascular deconditioning, orthostatic intolerance, decreased exercise capacity). In-mission countermeasures and monitoring have been implemented, and available evidence from current missions in Low Earth Orbit (LEO) suggest that functional impairments recover in the weeks/months after landing with a reconditioning program. Less is known following missions >1 year, and there is minimal experience with missions beyond LEO (>14 days) or in partial gravity (>3 days). Epidemiological evidence does not support an increased lifetime risk of cardiovascular disease death in astronauts, but mission durations have been limited largely to 4-6 months and there has been limited follow-up. A statistical increase in atherosclerosis-related cardiovascular pathologies are observed at late time points when exposed to ionizing radiation (e.g., gamma-rays and x-rays) at and above 500 milligray (mGy) terrestrially in human. 2018 National Council on Radiation Protection (NCRP) guidance states “there is not sufficient evidence that absorbed doses in the heart ≤0.5 Gy cause CVDs” (in the context of terrestrial radiation protection) and that the underlying mechanisms are still unclear which makes modeling these effects difficult. Age, sleep, exercise, diet, and stress are known contributors to cardiovascular disease. Resource limitations will affect medical capability and clinical outcomes in mission, particularly in missions at a greater distance from Earth. Mitigation Strategy The strategy for understanding and mitigating spaceflight-induced cardiovascular effects is stepwise and includes: 1) Characterization of the effects of long duration weightlessness and radiation exposure, separately and in combination, through experimentation/research and occupational health monitorin g, 2) development , testing and validation of countermeasures in ground, analog, and low-Earth orbit tests, and finally 3) countermeasure validation in the deep spaceflight environment (Gateway and Artemis). To characterize and understand the effects of each spaceflight hazard (altered gravity, radiation, isolation and confinement, hostile closed environment, and distance from Earth) alone and in combination, ground-based analogs, animal models, and human subjects testing will be used (e.g., bed rest, hindlimb suspension, parabolic flight), as well as long-duration spaceflight opportunities to study cells, tissues, animals, and humans exposed to the conditions of LEO. Because experimental radiation studies are generally limited to in-vitro and animal models, the effects of space radiation (thresholds, dose-responses and the effects of chronic or protracted dose-rates) in isolation and in combination with other spaceflight hazards will be characterized using: 1) long-term astronaut occupational surveillance, 2) by leveraging data from human radiotherapy patients and previously flown astronauts of various durations, and 3) by using current and developing new animal, cell culture, and organ-on-a-chip models for ground-based laboratory studies using space radiation analogs (e.g. NSRL). Additionally, monitoring of astronauts during and after Artemis missions also will be conducted. An emerging medical concern is thrombosis during spaceflight, particularly in the internal jugular vein. Though only one case has been documented, it does not preclude that there have been previous cases that were undetected. Characterization of the incidence of thrombosis and definition of the contributing factors that result in a venous thrombus are high priorities. Confirmation or revision of current preflight screening practices, surveillance activities, and interventions as well as development of countermeasures are of great importance to crew health and mission success, particularly for crewed missions beyond Earth orbit. Countermeasures against orthostatic intolerance (OI) are used operationally to protect crew upon return to Earth, but whether countermeasures are required to protect the crew during head-to-foot accelerations experienced during descent to and ascent from an extraterrestrial surface is not defined. An investigation of OI in males and females with and without lower body compression garments during varying simulated gravity levels is ongoing . The results of this study will help inform the standards and requirements defining the acceleration limits for the Human Landing System Program with and without compression garment and whether additional OI countermeasures may be needed. Candidate c ountermeasure identification and development for non-orthostatic intolerance concerns rely upon data mining, monitoring emerging research and developments highlighted at conferences, literature review, the NASA process of Request for Information (RFI), studies using human iPSCs (human-induced pluripotent stem cell), and workshops and technical interchange meetings (TIM) with key experts. Countermeasure testing will be conducted on the ground in established animal models and human subject-relevant spaceflight analogs followed by demonstration of countermeasure efficacy in ISS astronauts. Data collection on astronauts during and after Artemis missions using the suggested countermeasures will complete the mitigation strategy.

title: Risk of Mission Performance Decrements and Adverse Health Outcomes Resulting from Reduced Cardiorespiratory and Musculoskeletal Fitness
prompt: Explain NASA HRP Risk #180 (Muscle and Aerobic): Risk of Mission Performance Decrements and Adverse Health Outcomes Resulting from Reduced Cardiorespiratory and Musculoskeletal Fitness, its mission ratings, and clinical context.
response:
HRP Element: Human Health Countermeasures (HHC). Risk Statement: Given that exposure to a reduced gravity environment causes cardio-respiratory (e.g., maximal oxygen consumption and ventilatory threshold) and musculoskeletal fitness (e.g., strength, power, and endurance) to decline, there is a risk of impaired mission task performance and adverse health outcomes. Note: This risk is carried as two separate risks at the HSRB. The content in this field has been developed by HRP. HSRB State of Knowledge Despite the use of inflight exercise countermeasures on the International Space Station (ISS), current evidence suggests that cardio-respiratory and musculoskeletal fitness decrease during spaceflight and after spaceflight, though individual variability is evident that cannot be fully explained by countermeasure adherence. During ISS missions, some astronauts do not meet the current fitness standards for operations in weightlessness, and many astronauts would not meet current fitness standards for extravehicular operations on celestial surfaces. Further, many have not returned to preflight fitness levels by the end of the standard reconditioning program (30 days after landing). Limited data exist for astronauts who participate in spaceflight missions greater than the standard ISS mission duration (4-6 months), for women astronauts, and during and after partial gravity exposures. In long-duration missions on ISS, astronauts have access for a robust suite of exercise countermeasures (cycle ergometer, treadmill, resistive exercise) but countermeasure capabilities likely will be reduced for exploration missions due to mass, volume, and power limitations. As the design and architecture of future exploration missions evolve (e.g., vehicle design, spacesuit design, mission objectives), characterization of physical requirements to perform critical tasks and of crew health in these novel mission scenarios is required to inform and refine the requirements for countermeasures against cardio-respiratory and musculoskeletal deconditioning and the physical fitness standards which these countermeasures are intended to support. Note: This risk is carried as two separate risks at the HSRB. The content in this field has been developed by HRP. Mitigation Strategy Extended duration spaceflight mission studies and evaluations of novel exercise systems on ISS, Orion, and Gateway as well as in spaceflight or ground analogs are planned to help inform this risk for exploration class missions, including Mars mission parameters. EVA task-specific evaluations will include assessment of the fitness levels required to successfully perform mission tasks. This includes measuring metabolic costs and muscle strength requirements of critical tasks and of individual factors contributing to task success (e.g., anthropometry, hydration and caloric intake, fatigue, and sex). Operational Relevance: If muscle and/or cardio-respiratory fitness are below levels required to perform mission critical tasks then the crew are at higher risks for compromised performance capabilities. The compromised capabilities could impact the ability to complete mission objectives and result in decreased mission efficiency and efficacy, or increased risk for injury or other health impacts. Programs need to provide adequate exercise systems and time to perform the exercise to maintain performance capabilities across all phases of the mission (pre-, in-, and post-flight). HRP needs to provide the SME knowledge and contribute to the data needs to develop programmatic exercise system requirements.

title: Blood Glucose (Fasting / Pre-Post Exercise)
prompt: How is Blood Glucose (Fasting / Pre-Post Exercise) measured in space, what are nominal vs critical thresholds, and what countermeasures apply?
response: Unit: mg/dL. Nominal: 70 - 99. Caution: 62 - 69 or 100 - 189. Critical: < 62 or > 190. Microgravity Effect: Unloading of postural muscles (soleus/quadriceps) reduces GLUT4-mediated glucose uptake and induces spaceflight-associated insulin resistance. Space Measurement: Finger-prick micro-glucometer or wearable continuous interstitial glucose sensor; verified via Inspiration4 CMP (OSD-575). Countermeasure: Daily high-intensity ergometer + ARED resistance workouts; balanced low-glycemic spaceflight nutrition; hydration check.

title: Arterial Blood Pressure (Systolic / Diastolic)
prompt: How is Arterial Blood Pressure (Systolic / Diastolic) measured in space, what are nominal vs critical thresholds, and what countermeasures apply?
response: Unit: mmHg. Nominal: 95-120 / 60-80. Caution: 85-94 or 121-159 / 52-59 or 81-99. Critical: SBP < 85 or > 160; DBP < 52 or > 100. Microgravity Effect: Cephalad fluid shift (1.5-2 L from legs to thorax/head) raises upper-body vascular pressure in orbit and causes post-flight orthostatic intolerance. Space Measurement: Oscillometric arm cuff held strictly at heart level while stationary for 60s; Doppler ultrasound for jugular flow. Countermeasure: Lower Body Negative Pressure (LBNP) device, fluid-loading electrolyte protocol before re-entry, aerobic cycling.

title: Resting Heart Rate
prompt: How is Resting Heart Rate measured in space, what are nominal vs critical thresholds, and what countermeasures apply?
response: Unit: bpm. Nominal: 55 - 90. Caution: 45-54 or 91-115. Critical: < 45 or > 120 (at rest). Microgravity Effect: Cardiac remodeling, reduced plasma volume (10-15%), and altered autonomic baroreflex sensitivity increase arrhythmia/tachycardia risk. Space Measurement: 12-lead ECG, chest-strap telemetry, or optical PPG wearable; linked to radiation cardiac studies (OSD-435). Countermeasure: Daily cardiovascular ergometer conditioning, electrolyte balance, 12-lead ECG uplink during chest pain/palpitations.

title: Core Body Temperature
prompt: How is Core Body Temperature measured in space, what are nominal vs critical thresholds, and what countermeasures apply?
response: Unit: °C. Nominal: 36.2 - 37.3. Caution: 35.5-36.1 or 37.4-38.2. Critical: < 35.4 or > 38.3. Microgravity Effect: Absence of convective cooling and sweat pooling causes 'Space Fever' (+0.5 to +1.0°C baseline elevation during exercise/rest). Space Measurement: Temporal artery forehead thermometer or ingestible telemetry pill. Countermeasure: Increase cabin airflow fans, liquid-cooling ventilation garment (LCVG) during EVA, check infection/latent viral reactivation.

title: Blood Oxygen Saturation (SpO2)
prompt: How is Blood Oxygen Saturation (SpO2) measured in space, what are nominal vs critical thresholds, and what countermeasures apply?
response: Unit: %. Nominal: 95 - 100. Caution: 91 - 94. Critical: < 90. Microgravity Effect: Mild hypoxemia risks during EVA prebreathe, decompression events, or Lunar/Mars reduced-pressure habitat atmospheres (8.2 psi / 34% O2). Space Measurement: Fingertip pulse oximetry + cabin PPO2/CO2 ECLSS telemetry. Countermeasure: Immediate supplemental O2 (4 L/min), verify cabin O2/CO2 scrubbers, screen for decompression sickness (DCS) symptoms.

title: Daily Sleep Duration & Circadian Alignment
prompt: How is Daily Sleep Duration & Circadian Alignment measured in space, what are nominal vs critical thresholds, and what countermeasures apply?
response: Unit: hours/day. Nominal: 6.5 - 8.5. Caution: 4.5 - 6.4. Critical: < 4.5. Microgravity Effect: 16 orbital sunrises/sunsets per 24h, cabin noise, CO2 pockets, and workload shifts cause chronic sleep debt and circadian desynchronization. Space Measurement: Wrist actigraphy, sleep logs, and PVT cognitive reaction testing. Countermeasure: Blue-enriched morning / amber evening solid-state lighting, sleep-station airflow fans, CBT-I & scheduled wind-down.

title: Behavioral Health & Mood Score (PHQ-9 / Stress Scale)
prompt: How is Behavioral Health & Mood Score (PHQ-9 / Stress Scale) measured in space, what are nominal vs critical thresholds, and what countermeasures apply?
response: Unit: 1-4 scale (1=Optimal, 4=Severe). Nominal: 1. Caution: 2 - 3. Critical: 4. Microgravity Effect: Prolonged isolation, confinement, crew friction, and communication delay (>22 min one-way to Mars) elevate anxiety, depression, and cognitive fatigue. Space Measurement: Self-report mood check-ins, speech/facial affect biomarkers, and computerized cognitive batteries. Countermeasure: Private family audio/video conferences, autonomous psychological support tools, workload balancing, structured recreation.

title: Postural Stability & Sensorimotor Balance Score
prompt: How is Postural Stability & Sensorimotor Balance Score measured in space, what are nominal vs critical thresholds, and what countermeasures apply?
response: Unit: % (0-100). Nominal: 82 - 100. Caution: 62 - 81.9. Critical: < 62. Microgravity Effect: Otolith unloading and proprioceptive reweighting cause space motion sickness in orbit and severe postural ataxia upon gravity transitions (Moon/Mars/Earth). Space Measurement: Computerized MediaPipe Pose sway kinematics, tandem walk, and sit-to-stand balance tests. Countermeasure: Vestibular adaptation exercises, handrail anchoring, Promethazine for acute SMS, sensorimotor reconditioning before EVA.

title: Bilateral Joint Kinematics Symmetry Difference
prompt: How is Bilateral Joint Kinematics Symmetry Difference measured in space, what are nominal vs critical thresholds, and what countermeasures apply?
response: Unit: degrees. Nominal: 0.0 - 4.5. Caution: 4.6 - 13.0. Critical: > 13.0. Microgravity Effect: Asymmetric musculoskeletal deconditioning, EVA suit shoulder/hand strain, or intervertebral disc swelling (spinal elongation) causes kinematic asymmetry. Space Measurement: Real-time pose landmark joint angle symmetry (left vs right shoulder, hip, knee) via onboard camera. Countermeasure: Balanced ARED resistance loading, spinal decompression stretching, EVA suit fit verification.

title: Ocular Fatigue (EAR) & SANS Neuro-Ocular Status
prompt: How is Ocular Fatigue (EAR) & SANS Neuro-Ocular Status measured in space, what are nominal vs critical thresholds, and what countermeasures apply?
response: Unit: EAR ratio / IOP mmHg. Nominal: EAR >= 0.235 | IOP 10-21 mmHg. Caution: EAR 0.195 - 0.234. Critical: EAR < 0.195 or IOP > 22 mmHg / acute visual acuity drop. Microgravity Effect: Headward fluid shift elevates intracranial/choroidal pressure, causing optic disc edema, globe flattening, choroidal folds, and hyperopic shift (SANS). Space Measurement: FaceMesh Eye Aspect Ratio (EAR) for fatigue + In-flight OCT, Fundoscopy, Tonometry IOP, and ocular ultrasound (OSD-583/679). Countermeasure: LBNP fluid redistribution, B-vitamin/one-carbon metabolic supplementation, corrective Space Anticipation Glasses, OCT tracking.

title: Space Radiation Dose Rate & Cumulative Exposure (GCR / SPE / Neutrons)
prompt: How is Space Radiation Dose Rate & Cumulative Exposure (GCR / SPE / Neutrons) measured in space, what are nominal vs critical thresholds, and what countermeasures apply?
response: Unit: mSv / day (or mSv cumulative). Nominal: < 1.0 mSv/day (LEO ~0.4-0.8 mSv/day). Caution: 1.0 - 10.0 mSv/day (Deep space GCR ~1.5-2.0 mSv/day). Critical: > 50 mSv/hr (SPE Solar Particle Event) or > 600 mSv career limit. Microgravity Effect: GCR high-Z/energy ions and secondary neutrons (~30% of ISS dose per CSA CANS) damage DNA, elevate lifetime cancer risk, and injure CNS/cardiovascular tissue. Space Measurement: Active dosimeters (RAD), CSA Canadian Active Neutron Spectrometer (CANS), Radi-N2 bubble detectors, crew personal badges. Countermeasure: Retreat to Aft Water Wall / polyethylene storm shelter during SPE, abort EVA within 8 min, log personal dosimeter rates.

title: Cabin CO2 Partial Pressure (ppCO2)
prompt: How is Cabin CO2 Partial Pressure (ppCO2) measured in space, what are nominal vs critical thresholds, and what countermeasures apply?
response: Unit: mmHg. Nominal: < 2.0. Caution: 2.0 - 3.9. Critical: >= 4.0. Microgravity Effect: Closed ECLSS habitats accumulate CO2 pockets around crew without airflow, causing headaches, cognitive impairment, hypercapnia, and exacerbating SANS. Space Measurement: Continuous ECLSS CO2 infrared analyzers + transcutaneous pCO2 monitoring. Countermeasure: Verify CDRA/amine scrubber status, maximize sleep-station ventilation fans, inspect filters for lunar/martian dust.

Canadian science on the International Space Station
Canada's participation in the International Space Station ( ISS ) allows our scientists to access the unique space environment and conduct cutting-edge experiments aboard the orbiting laboratory to:

more time in weightlessness

title: Monitoring radiation for astronaut health
prompt: Summarize Canadian Space Agency (CSA) insights on: Monitoring radiation for astronaut health
response:
Canadian Space Agency ( CSA ) astronaut David Saint-Jacques using bubble detectors, a predecessor to Canadian Active Neutron Spectrometer (CANS), on the International Space Station ( ISS ). (Credits: CSA / NASA )
Radiation is one of the key challenges faced by astronauts living and working beyond the protective shield of Earth’s atmosphere. As Canada and its international partners advance plans for missions to the Moon, and eventually Mars, the CSA continues to invest in technology to better understand exposure levels.
The CSA has awarded a contract of $5.5 million to Bubble Technology Industries for the continued development of the CANS , a compact and autonomous instrument designed to measure neutron radiation exposure in space.
Neutron radiation, which contributes to about 30% of total radiation on the ISS , is especially harmful because it can cause serious biological damage and require specialized protective measures. For over 25 years, the ISS has been a test bed for new technology. Canada has significant expertise in radiation detection experiments on the ISS , including MOSFET , EVARM and Radi-N and Radi-N2 .
CANS improves upon previous radiation detection methods with the unique combined capabilities of working continuously and autonomously. Data collected could help develop better measures to reduce risks for astronauts’ health and also has potential applications on Earth, including cancer therapy, radiation protection for aircrews, nuclear threat detection and public safety, among others.

title: Acute Protocol: Coronary & Angina Triage
prompt: What is the spaceflight emergency protocol for chest-pain (trigger: Acute chest pain, resting HR > 120 bpm, SBP > 180 or < 85 mmHg)?
response:
[CODE RED - CRITICAL] Acute Protocol: Coronary & Angina Triage:
- Halt all physical exercise (ergometer/ARED) immediately and secure crew member in sleep station harness.
- Deploy Clinical Medical Pack Alpha: Initiate 12-lead ECG telemetry stream to Flight Surgeon console.
- Administer supplemental oxygen via oral-nasal mask at 4 L/min.
- Verify astronaut has not consumed sildenafil or PDE-5 inhibitors; prepare chewable Aspirin 325 mg.
- Maintain direct voice link with Houston Flight Surgeon on Air-to-Ground 1 (or autonomous protocol if Mars comms delay > 5 min).

title: Acute Protocol: Presyncope & Orthostatic Instability
prompt: What is the spaceflight emergency protocol for dizziness (trigger: Presyncope, SBP < 90 mmHg, post-landing/gravity transition dizziness)?
response:
[URGENT - TIER 2] Acute Protocol: Presyncope & Orthostatic Instability:
- Secure astronaut in supine position with feet elevated to alleviate cephalic hypoperfusion.
- Administer 1.0 L oral electrolyte rehydration solution within 60 minutes.
- Check continuous blood pressure cuff every 5 minutes for postural hypotension.
- Verify cabin CO2 levels on ECLSS sensor (ensure < 2.5 mmHg partial pressure).
- Activate lower-body compression garment / LBNP countermeasure if transitioning gravity fields.

title: Acute Protocol: Vestibular Ataxia & Otolith Decompensation
prompt: What is the spaceflight emergency protocol for balance-loss (trigger: Balance score < 62%, joint asymmetry > 13°, acute vertigo/nausea)?
response:
[OBSERVATION] Acute Protocol: Vestibular Ataxia & Otolith Decompensation:
- Anchor crew member to primary handrails to prevent rotational tumble and head impact.
- Restrict rapid head movements in pitch and yaw axes (mitigate Coriolis effect).
- Administer Promethazine 25mg IM or oral if accompanied by active space motion sickness (SMS).
- Inspect cabin air intake filters for particulate, Lunar/Mars dust, or chemical irritants.

title: Acute Protocol: Solar Particle Event (SPE) Alert
prompt: What is the spaceflight emergency protocol for radiation (trigger: SPE flux > 50 mSv/hr or CANS/RAD dosimeter surge alert)?
response:
[RADIATION SHELTER] Acute Protocol: Solar Particle Event (SPE) Alert:
- Immediately sound habitat klaxon: all crew retreat to Aft Water Wall / polyethylene storm shelter.
- Terminate ongoing Extravehicular Activities (EVA) within 8-minute airlock contingency window.
- Record active personal dosimeter (RAD) and CSA CANS neutron spectrometer readings immediately.
- Deploy auxiliary polyethylene shielding blankets over crew bunk positions.
- Await Space Radiation Analysis Group (SRAG) real-time flux clearance before resuming EVA.

title: Acute Protocol: Hypoxia / Decompression Sickness (DCS) Triage
prompt: What is the spaceflight emergency protocol for hypoxia-dcs (trigger: SpO2 < 90%, cabin depressurization, joint pain ('bends') post-EVA)?
response:
[CODE RED - EVA / CABIN] Acute Protocol: Hypoxia / Decompression Sickness (DCS) Triage:
- Don emergency 100% O2 mask or seal EVA suit pressure loop immediately.
- Verify cabin total pressure, PPO2, and ppCO2 on ECLSS console.
- If DCS suspected post-EVA, initiate hyperbaric treatment protocol (suit/airlock repressurization + 100% O2).
- Log neurological exam, pulse oximetry, and vital signs every 5 minutes.

title: Acute Protocol: SANS Visual Acuity & Intracranial Pressure Shift
prompt: What is the spaceflight emergency protocol for sans-vision (trigger: Acute hyperopic shift, scotoma, IOP > 22 mmHg, or sustained EAR < 0.195)?
response:
[CLINICAL ALERT] Acute Protocol: SANS Visual Acuity & Intracranial Pressure Shift:
- Perform in-flight Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT), Fundoscopy, and Tonometry IOP check.
- Measure visual acuity using onboard Amsler grid and Space Anticipation Glasses calibration.
- Check cabin ppCO2 (< 2.0 mmHg target, as elevated CO2 worsens cerebral vasodilation).
- Schedule LBNP session and review one-carbon / B-complex nutritional status.
